description: Our plan: use NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data to tell the story of a changing landscape in Tajikistan — melting and moving glaciers in the Pamir mountains, changing water levels in reservoirs and lakes, and ground deformation in one of the most seismically active regions in Central Asia. We'll turn complex radar observations into an interactive web map with before/after sliders, time-series animations and a clear story anyone can understand.
summary: Surface Pulse is an open-source web app that turns NISAR L-band radar into stories anyone can follow, with no radar knowledge needed. It tells four real changes from 2026 in English, Russian and Tajik. Two reservoirs on Tajikistan's Vakhsh River fill up: Nurek grows from 74.3 to 89.7 km² and Rogun from 13.9 to 20.0 km². The ground at the Rogun dam is measured for movement with InSAR (preliminary). Crops grow and are harvested in the Vakhsh valley. A flood hits Nepal's Bhote Koshi–Trishuli valley on 26 August 2026 and is mapped under monsoon cloud. For each story the app answers what changed, where, why, and how sure we are. It has change maps, a time-lapse of every 12-day pass, a camera-vs-radar swipe, a click-anywhere verdict, and a measured answer to which polarization works best (HH for water, HV for plants). This matters because NISAR sees through clouds, day and night, but its data are hard to read. Surface Pulse makes them understandable for water managers, decision-makers, teachers and the people who live in these valleys, and it is honest about the limits of the data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Surface Pulse explains surface change seen by NISAR to people who have never used radar data. A landing page shows in plain words how radar sees water, rock and plants. A radar beam sweeps the clouds off a real NISAR picture, because radar sees through clouds.

The map has four stories, each with the tabs What changed / Why / Can we trust it / What to do, and a step-by-step Guide:

- Lakes: the Rogun and Nurek reservoirs on the Vakhsh River, Tajikistan (27 Jun – 13 Oct 2026: Nurek 74.3 → 89.7 km², Rogun 13.9 → 20.0 km²; Rogun's estimated water level about 1,115 → 1,128 m, ±10 m).

- Ground movement at Rogun (InSAR, preliminary): the dam area stays within about ±3 cm; one 0.36 km² slope moved +11.6 cm along the radar line of sight.

- Crops in the Vakhsh valley: over ~696 km² of flat fields the plant echo (HV) rose 1.3 dB from June to September; by 6 November, 28–54 km² dropped sharply (candidate harvested fields).

- Flood in Nepal (Bhote Koshi–Trishuli, 26 Aug 2026): mapped under monsoon cloud, with a 10 m close-up of the lower valley. The app also shows what is NOT the flood: most of the brightening is the river shrinking after the monsoon.

Main views:

- What changed? (change map)

- Watch it happen (time-lapse of 11–13 passes, 12 days apart)

- Before / after swipe, including Camera vs radar: over Nepal the photo is mostly cloud, while the radar shows the valley floor

- Click anywhere for "What happened at this place?": a one-sentence verdict and the history of that spot

- "Which radar channel is best?": HH vs HV measured live on the changed pixels

- One river, one pulse: the Vakhsh seen from the side, 257 km; one timeline moves the Rogun level, the Nurek area and the crop signal together, with NASA POWER weather

- A dashboard with automatic "what needs attention" notes

- A printable one-page report per story

- Advice for water managers, decision-makers, scientists, teachers and the public

HOW IT WORKS

- NISAR L2 GCOV (terrain-corrected radar backscatter) is cut to each site and averaged to 60 m.

- Lakes = pixels dark in both HH and HV, within a height range from the Copernicus DEM, connected to the lake.

- Farmland = flat fields (slope < 2°), followed with the median HV.

- Flood = before/after HH change on the valley floors.

- Ground movement comes from the team's own stack of 8 consecutive 12-day NISAR L2 GUNW (InSAR) pairs.

- Optical photos (NASA HLS, within ±6 days of each pass) and NASA POWER weather explain the "why".

- Context (rivers, villages with population, dams) comes from OpenStreetMap.

- Change detection runs in the browser.

Every new date was added only after the processing reproduced an existing date (e.g. HV r = 0.9986; Nurek area within ±2.4%). Our pictures were also checked against ASF's own NISAR browse images, and every headline number was audited.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Tajikistan: Nurek produces about half to 70% of the country's electricity (sources differ), and Rogun's filling means resettlement (up to 42,000 people). NISAR sees these lakes every 12 days through cloud, and the app shows it in Tajik and Russian, not only English.

- Disasters: the Nepal story shows radar mapping a flood when cameras see only cloud, and it separates real flood signals from seasonal change.

- Farming and infrastructure: harvest candidates, and dam and slope monitoring with InSAR.

- Learning: anyone can understand the change, read why it happened, and judge how reliable it is.

CREATIVITY

- "One river, one pulse" links lakes, power and fields on one river profile and one timeline.

- "Hear the pulse": every satellite pass is a heartbeat; louder = more change (sound off by default).

- Camera vs radar on the same pass makes "radar sees through clouds" visible in one swipe.

- The app speaks the language of the people who live by the Vakhsh.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: data are PROVISIONAL/VALIDATED NISAR products, and the first Nepal passes are from the experimental release (checked identical on one pass). NISAR has a data gap from 27 Jul to 10 Aug 2026. The InSAR result is preliminary. Nurek's 6 Nov area is flagged as rough water after rain. The harvest area is given as a range because of a processing-version offset. Amplitude maps are never presented as centimetre ground movement.

- Accessibility: plain words, a Simple mode and an Expert mode, three languages, a phone layout.

- Open source: MIT licence; NISAR data are free.

TOOLS

JavaScript, React 18, Vite 5, MapLibre GL 4.7, Chart.js 4.4, react-router-dom; Python (numpy, h5py, scipy, scikit-image, pyproj); Node.js scripts; GitHub Pages.

USE OF AI

We used Claude (Anthropic) through Claude Code as a coding assistant for the app and the data scripts, and to draft the interface text and its Russian and Tajik translations. No data, measurement or picture in the app was generated by AI. All numbers come from NISAR, Copernicus DEM, HLS and NASA POWER data through scripts in our repository. The team is responsible for the science and the conclusions.
dataRefs: NASA ARSET: Monitoring Surface Water with SAR (2026)
